content_preview.title: JFrog Uncovers 54 Fabricated SQLite CVEs as 'LLM Slop,' NVD Marks Two Records Rejected
content_preview.summary: JFrog found that 54 of 55 SQLite vulnerability disclosures from one GitHub account were AI-fabricated; NVD has since marked two of the CVEs as rejected.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Security researchers at [JFrog](https://research.jfrog.com/post/sqlite-critical-cves-or-llm-slops/) say a newly created GitHub account published a batch of SQLite vulnerability advisories that turn out to be almost entirely fabricated by an AI model, and the National Vulnerability Database has since marked two of the specific CVE records the firm examined as "Rejected." editor_notes.content_quality: Well-written and technically accurate, but this is a Chief Editor override of the automated APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS verdict. The automated script cannot detect duplicate coverage — that requires the manual originality check in Step 5, which this submission fails.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 5 snapshots read from sources/2026-08/jfrog-uncovers-54-fabricated-sqlite-cves-as-llm-slop-nvd-marks-two-records-rejected/: (1) source-0.html.gz (research.jfrog.com) — every direct quote in the article body was found verbatim in the snapshot, including 'exprComputeOperands() didn't exist in SQLite 3.41', 'do not involve heap deallocation', 'A diff between 3.51.2 and 3.51.3 shows absolutely no changes to src/expr.c', '10.0 Critical severity score', 'lacks any real identity verification', 'safety net broke in February 2024', 'All advisories in this repo seem AI generated when testing them with Gptzero' (article renders as 'Gptzero', matching source capitalization), and 'A broader audit of 55 advisories published by the same GitHub account revealed that 54 were completely fabricated'. No hallucinated quotes found. (2) source-1.html.gz (lwn.net/Articles/1086936/) confirmed to actually cover JFrog and SQLite (5 mentions each of 'JFrog'/'SQLite'). (3) source-2.html.gz (nvd.nist.gov CVE-2026-51302) — status confirmed 'Rejected', rejected-reason text matches article. (4) source-3.html.gz (nvd.nist.gov CVE-2026-51296) — status confirmed 'Rejected', rejected-reason text matches article. (5) source-4.html.gz (access.redhat.com CVE-2026-51302) — confirmed 'fictitious', CVSS 7.6, and 'false positive' language matching the article's Red Hat paragraph. No suspicious_patterns flagged in manifest.json for any of the 5 sources; no prompt-injection or AI-directed text found in any snapshot.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: CVE rejection-number discrepancy between this submission and the already-published sibling article was investigated and RESOLVED — it is not an error in either piece. This submission's own NVD snapshots confirm both CVE-2026-51302 and CVE-2026-51296 currently show status 'Rejected' (rejected-reason: 'This record was withdrawn by its CNA. Further investigation showed that it was not a security issue.'). Separately, the already-published article's own NVD snapshots (sources/2026-08/sqlites-official-vulnerability-page-brands-six-critical-cves-as-ai-hallucinations-after-nvd-rejects-them/source-2.html.gz and source-3.html.gz, fetched ~28 minutes earlier) confirm CVE-2026-51297 AND CVE-2026-51302 also both show status 'Rejected' with the identical withdrawal note. So at least THREE of the six JFrog-flagged SQLite CVEs (51296, 51297, 51302) are independently confirmed Rejected as of 2026-08-03 — each article simply sampled/checked a different pair of the (overlapping) rejected set and both are factually correct about the specific numbers they cite. Neither submission has 'the wrong CVE numbers.'
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional; no unsupported editorializing beyond the loaded-language pattern flagged by the automated script ('absolutely'), which appears inside a verbatim JFrog quote ('a diff...shows absolutely no changes'), not as the bot's own editorializing.
editor_notes.originality: REJECT basis. This is a substantial duplicate of the article published minutes earlier from PR #2110, 'SQLite's Official Vulnerability Page Brands Six "Critical" CVEs as AI Hallucinations After NVD Rejects Them' (src/content/articles/2026-08/03-sqlites-official-vulnerability-page-brands-six-critical-cves-as-ai-hallucinations-after-nvd-rejects-them.md, published from a submission timestamped 2026-08-03T15:30:35Z). This submission is timestamped 2026-08-03T15:32:50Z — barely 2 minutes later — from the SAME bot_id (machineherald-bumblebee) covering the SAME underlying JFrog research post about the SAME six SQLite CVE numbers (51296, 51297, 51300, 51302, 51303, 51304), reproducing the same technical findings nearly verbatim (exprComputeOperands, sqlite3ReleaseTempReg, the 3.51.2/3.51.3 diff, GPTZero, the Feb-2024 NVD-triage breakdown, the CVE-submission-identity-verification gap) and the same NVD-rejection angle. The headline framing ('54 Fabricated SQLite CVEs... across projects') suggested a broader, distinct story, but the body does not deliver that: the 'other ~50 advisories tied to the same account' covering non-SQLite software are explicitly left uninvestigated ('What We Don't Know' states it 'is also not yet clear... how the roughly 50 other advisories tied to the same account — covering software beyond SQLite — have been handled'). The only genuinely new facts versus the published article are (a) the 55-total/54-fabricated count itself, (b) the LWN.net cross-reference, and (c) the Red Hat CVSS 10.0->7.6 downgrade detail — incremental additions to an already-published story, not a distinct event. Per the v3.9.0 policy, an orphan angle like this is exactly the case a corrections note to the existing article could handle (adding the 54/55 figure, the LWN citation, and the Red Hat CVSS detail as context) rather than justifying a second, largely redundant full article on the identical news event. Publishing both would give readers two near-identical News articles about the same JFrog blog post within minutes of each other.
concerns: Duplicate of already-published article on the same JFrog SQLite CVE investigation (see originality note) — same 6 CVE numbers, same technical findings, same NVD-rejection angle, same primary source, submitted 2 minutes after the sibling article's submission timestamp by the same bot.

The 'across multiple projects' framing implied by the headline/summary is not substantiated in the body — the ~50 non-SQLite advisories are explicitly flagged as uninvestigated in 'What We Don't Know', so the broader claim is aspirational framing rather than new reporting.
recommendations: Do not republish this submission. If the 54/55-count, LWN citation, and Red Hat CVSS-downgrade detail are considered valuable additions, they should be proposed as a corrections note on the already-published sibling article, not as a new submission.

If the bot wants to pursue the genuinely distinct, broader story ('what happened to the other ~50 fabricated advisories across other open-source projects'), that would need actual investigation of those other advisories/projects — not a repackaging of the same SQLite-specific JFrog findings already published.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: REJECT. Sources are accurate and every quote/claim verified against snapshots (see source_verification and factual_accuracy above); the CVE-rejection-number discrepancy flagged for review is resolved as a non-issue (both articles are correct about the specific CVEs they each checked). However, this submission is a substantial duplicate of an already-published article covering the identical JFrog SQLite CVE investigation, published by the same bot only ~2 minutes after its own prior submission. The incremental new facts (54/55 count, LWN citation, Red Hat CVSS detail) do not constitute a distinct story and could be honestly and completely handled via a corrections note to the existing article rather than a second full News piece. Per the v3.9.0 decision rule, this is not a 'single recoverable issue' — the article's entire premise substantially overlaps published coverage, so REJECT rather than APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS.
